[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

The infrastructure module is one of five mandatory components of a Golden Path bundle, but no specification defines what workload infrastructure it must provision or what outputs it must expose. Without a specification, Platform Engineering authors each path's infrastructure module ad hoc — provision content varies between paths, security-bearing configurations are sometimes left as consumer-supplied inputs rather than path constants, output names and sensitivity declarations differ between paths, and the manifest file that allows ARB reviewers to verify completeness is frequently omitted. The security template cannot reference a workload identity credential that was not created with the correct scope; the application scaffold cannot configure a secrets store integration whose URI was not output by the module; the compliance metadata cannot declare infrastructure controls that were not encoded as path constants. An ad hoc infrastructure module means every new Golden Path requires individual Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture review of the same gaps before ARB approval — at the catalog level rather than the service level, but still per-path, per-review.
page_texts.5:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#solution-overview]

### Solution Overview

This pattern defines the mandatory structure, required provision categories, output contract, and policy check set that every Golden Path infrastructure module must satisfy. A conforming module stored at `catalog/infrastructure/{path-id}/` provisions the workload isolation boundary, workload identity binding, and resource attribution that every other bundle component depends on as path constants — and exposes these as four required outputs so that the security template, application scaffold, and compliance metadata authors receive exact, structured values rather than locating them ad hoc. Because the provision categories, path constraint encoding rules, output names, and six IaC plan policy checks (TF-001 through TF-006) are specified here, Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture review the specification once at the catalog level. Every path that conforms to this pattern inherits that review without individual module evaluation.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#when-to-use]

### When to Use

- Authoring the infrastructure module component for a new Golden Path bundle before ARB submission
- Auditing an existing path's infrastructure module for conformance with this specification prior to re-submission or compliance review
- Remediating a catalog infrastructure module whose ad hoc authoring produced gaps in bundle component integration (missing outputs, consumer-overridable path constants, absent manifest)
- Extending an existing infrastructure module when a path version update introduces a new compliance scope (ARC-AMPE, FedRAMP Moderate) or a new technology profile variant (EKS, GKE)

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#benefits]

### Benefits

- Platform Engineering has a complete specification for what the infrastructure module must provision and what outputs it must expose — ad hoc authoring judgment is replaced by a checkable standard, and the pre-submission checklist in GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001 verifies conformance before any architecture review is scheduled
- Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture review the specification once at the catalog level; every path whose module conforms to this pattern inherits that review without individual module re-evaluation
- The four required outputs are defined as part of the specification, so the security template and scaffold authors receive exact, named values from the module — bundle components integrate by contract, not by convention, and placeholder values in workload identity artifacts become a detectable pre-submission failure rather than a silent production incident
- Autonomous AI agents generating or instantiating Golden Path services receive a catalog entry backed by a validated infrastructure module — the constrained solution space the [Enterprise Golden Path Strategy](../../../strategy/white-papers/engineering/enterprise-golden-path-strategy.md) requires

## Target Audience

This pattern is intended for the following technical roles:

- **Platform Engineer** — authoring and maintaining Golden Path infrastructure modules in the catalog
- **Infrastructure Architect** — defining and reviewing infrastructure module specifications and TF check contracts
- **Security Engineer** — reviewing workload identity, isolation boundary, and role assignment configurations for compliance
- **DevOps Engineer** — integrating Golden Path infrastructure modules into CI/CD provisioning pipelines

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#business-context]

### Business Context

The [Enterprise Golden Path Strategy](../../../strategy/white-papers/engineering/enterprise-golden-path-strategy.md) defines the Golden Path catalog as the mechanism by which Platform Engineering delivers a constrained solution space for application development — one where autonomous AI agents and development teams can generate and instantiate cloud-native services without making individual security, compliance, or infrastructure decisions. The strategy defines the infrastructure module as one of five mandatory bundle components: *“Terraform module(s) defining compute, networking, storage, and IAM with Gainwell-standard security configurations pre-wired.”* Pre-wired means those configurations are path constants authored once by Platform Engineering, not consumer-supplied inputs that teams or agents override at service instantiation time.

When no specification defines what the infrastructure module must contain, Platform Engineering authors it ad hoc. The result is inconsistency across the catalog: some paths have the workload isolation boundary correctly configured as a path constant with the enforcement baseline active; others have isolation boundaries without the enforcement baseline declared, leaving workloads unprotected by default. Some paths have per-workload identity bindings; others reference shared platform identities. The security template and scaffold authors for those paths have no module outputs to reference as path constants — they either embed placeholder values (which produce silent failures at service instantiation) or block waiting for the infrastructure author to deliver values later. A catalog with inconsistently authored infrastructure modules cannot support the autonomous AI development workflow the strategy requires.

Gainwell operates in a heavily regulated environment (HIPAA, FedRAMP, ARC-AMPE, Medicaid). The compliance claims recorded in the compliance metadata file at the path level — and relied upon by ARB reviewers, audit teams, and automated compliance monitoring — depend on the infrastructure module having provisioned the correct workload isolation, identity, and tagging configuration. A path whose infrastructure module is incomplete does not satisfy its compliance claims; it provides documentation that asserts them. The infrastructure module is the foundational component where those claims are grounded in provisioned resources.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#technical-context]

### Technical Context

Golden Path infrastructure modules are stored at `catalog/infrastructure/{path-id}/` in the Golden Path Catalog repository — the same catalog structure that holds the security template at `catalog/security/{path-id}/`, the scaffold at `catalog/templates/{path-id}/`, the verification contract at `catalog/verification/{path-id}/`, and the compliance metadata at `catalog/compliance/{path-id}/`. The infrastructure module is invoked by the CI/CD pipeline during path provisioning; it produces the workload isolation boundary, cloud provider identity resource, identity binding, and least-privilege role assignment that the workload execution environment is built around.

The bundle authoring sequence is constrained by dependency: the infrastructure module must be authored and applied to a staging environment before the security template and scaffold authors can finalize their artifacts. The security template author needs the workload identity credential reference (e.g., managed identity client ID on AKS; IAM role ARN on EKS; function execution role ARN on Lambda) to embed as the path constant in the workload identity artifact. The scaffold author needs the secrets store reference to wire the secret management artifact. Neither author can complete their artifact with a real value until the infrastructure module has been applied and its outputs captured. This sequencing constraint means an ad hoc or incomplete infrastructure module does not just delay its own ARB review — it blocks the security template and scaffold authoring phases for the entire bundle.

Infrastructure module conformance is verified across the four layers defined in the [Enterprise Architecture Verification Strategy](../../../strategy/white-papers/engineering/enterprise-architecture-verification-strategy.md) and operationalized through the Verification Contract (PTN-GOV-AI-003). A conforming module must satisfy all four layers — not just Layer 1 and Layer 3:

- **Layer 1 — Structural Conformance Gate** (build time): Verifies that `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`, and `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` are present at `catalog/infrastructure/{path-id}/`. Runs automatically at the start of every CI/CD pipeline execution and blocks all downstream stages on failure. Presence does not verify content correctness — that is Layer 3's responsibility.

- **Layer 2 — Fitness Functions** (post-apply behavioral validation): For the infrastructure module, two fitness functions verify that the provision category decisions are correctly implemented in a real environment, not just structurally present in the Terraform plan. Both must pass before module outputs are declared deliverable:
  - **Layer 2a — Isolation baseline validation**: Inspect the provisioned isolation boundary resource and confirm the enforcement baseline configuration declared as a path constant is active. The specific inspection command is technology-profile-specific (e.g., Kubernetes: `kubectl get ns {namespace} --show-labels`; ECS: describe task definition security group rules; Lambda: get resource policy). Result saved as `isolation-baseline-{path-id}-{version}.txt`.
  - **Layer 2b — Workload identity chain test**: Deploy a test execution context using the provisioned `workload_identity_ref` value; confirm the identity can authenticate to the secrets store and retrieve a test secret without error. The specific mechanism is technology-profile-specific (e.g., Kubernetes + ESO: test pod with workload identity annotation confirms secret sync; Lambda: test invocation with execution role confirms Secrets Manager access). Result saved as `identity-chain-{path-id}-{version}.txt`.

- **Layer 3 — Policy-as-Code** (pre-deployment gate): OPA/Rego policies evaluate `terraform show -json` plan output before `terraform apply` runs. The Terraform plan checks defined in the path's Verification Contract assert that all three provision categories are correctly configured. This is a veto gate — a check failure blocks `terraform apply`. The infrastructure module author co-defines the check assertions with the Verification Contract author (GUID-GOV-IMPL-001): the infrastructure author knows the Terraform plan JSON field paths and resource type names; the Verification Contract author knows Rego. A module that passes all Verification Contract TF checks satisfies the infrastructure prerequisites for the security template, scaffold, and compliance metadata components.

- **Layer 4 — Runtime Monitors** (post-deployment, continuous): AWS Config, Azure Policy, or GCP Config rules compare deployed resource state against declared Terraform state on a continuous basis. Drift triggers an automated incident. A conforming module **enables** Layer 4 by design: the four required tags (`compliance_scope`, `path_id`, `environment`, `team`) and the identity resource naming convention that includes `path_id` are the attribution labels by which the runtime monitoring layer identifies which resources belong to which path. A module that applies tags inconsistently or omits `path_id` from identity resource names produces resources the runtime monitor cannot attribute — drift goes undetected.

The three mandatory provision categories and their corresponding OPA checks address the security and compliance baseline that every Gainwell workload namespace must satisfy. These categories implement Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) tenets from NIST SP 800-207 at the infrastructure layer and map to NIST SP 800-53 r5 controls that are the normative compliance framework under HIPAA, ARC-AMPE, and FedRAMP Moderate overlays:

| Infrastructure Provision Category | ZTA Tenet (NIST SP 800-207) | NIST 800-53 r5 Control(s) | TF Check(s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Workload Isolation Boundary | Assume Breach: Minimize blast radius | CM-6, CM-7 | TF-001, TF-005 |
| Workload Identity | Tenets 3, 6: Per-session dynamic identity; verify explicitly | IA-9, AC-6 | TF-002, TF-003, TF-004, TF-006 |
| Resource Attribution | ZTA Asset Inventory: Complete resource enumeration | CM-8 | TF-005 |

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#problem-details]

### Problem Details

Without an infrastructure module specification:

- **Isolation boundary exists without enforcement baseline active — ZTA blast radius unlimited by default**: An isolation boundary provisioned without its enforcement baseline configuration (e.g., Kubernetes: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` on the namespace; ECS: task isolation security group rules; Lambda: execution role scope constraints) is permissive by default — workloads can operate outside the intended execution constraint. The security template may attempt to apply the enforcement baseline at runtime, but a runtime artifact is not an infrastructure constant and can be missing without triggering a build failure. This violates ZTA's Assume Breach tenet (minimize blast radius) and NIST 800-53 r5 CM-7 (Least Functionality) at the infrastructure layer. TF-001 catches this at Terraform plan time — the correct place to enforce it before provisioning occurs.

- **Shared or missing workload identity — implicit identity trust violates ZTA Tenet 6**: Without a dedicated cloud provider identity scoped to the path, workloads run under the platform's default identity or a shared identity accumulated by multiple paths. A compromised workload can then impersonate every other service sharing the same identity. This violates ZTA Tenet 6 (verify explicitly — every workload has a scoped, attested identity) and NIST 800-53 r5 IA-9 (Service Identification and Authentication) and AC-6 (Least Privilege). The security template's workload identity artifact references the credential output — if no dedicated identity was created, this value is a placeholder that produces a silent authentication failure at service runtime.

- **Workload identity binding not scoped to the workload execution context — authentication fails silently**: Even when a cloud provider identity resource exists, without a binding that constrains the identity to the specific workload execution context (e.g., Kubernetes: federated identity credential bound to `system:serviceaccount:{namespace}:{service_name}`; Lambda: execution role trust policy scoped to the specific function ARN; ECS: task-level execution role), the cloud identity provider rejects the token exchange. The workload starts, but the secrets reconciliation fails silently — the workload has no secrets. The compliance claim that workload identity is active is false; the workload runs under no effective identity binding.

- **Over-privileged role assignment — least-privilege violated before first deployment**: Without an explicit role specification, infrastructure authors commonly assign a broadly permissive role for convenience (e.g., `Key Vault Administrator` or `Contributor` on Azure; `AdministratorAccess` on AWS). This violates NIST 800-53 r5 AC-6 (Least Privilege). The workload identity only needs read access to secrets — the role that allows creation, deletion, and policy changes is never required by a deployed service.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#forces-and-constraints]

### Forces and Constraints

- The infrastructure module must be provisioned and its outputs captured before the security template can be authored — the workload identity credential reference is a path constant embedded in the workload identity artifact and `security-template-manifest.yaml`. Module outputs are inputs to the security template authoring phase (GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001 Phase 6)
- The isolation enforcement level is a path constant that must match between the Terraform module (encoded as a resource attribute) and the security template (context validation OPA check TF-001). Changing the enforcement level in either location without changing the other produces a split-brain state that cannot be detected until a workload is deployed
- The workload identity binding scope must exactly match the workload execution context the security template will configure — if the execution context name is derived from a scaffold parameter (e.g., `${{ values.service_name }}`), the identity binding must use the same format. The specific binding format is technology-profile-specific (e.g., Kubernetes: `system:serviceaccount:{namespace}:{service_name}`; Lambda: function ARN condition in the trust policy)
- Terraform state for the infrastructure module is stored in the environment-scoped state backend, not in the service repository. The module is invoked once per path-environment pair, not once per service instantiation. Consumer services pass `service_name` and `team` as inputs; all security-bearing values are path constants
- Registry module versioning (semver pinning) is required — consumers must not reference `source = "registry.terraform.io/gainwell/gp-001-infra"` without an explicit version pin. A CI/CD pipeline that auto-resolves to `latest` can silently adopt a breaking module change
- **AU family controls are out of scope for the workload infrastructure module**: Audit logging pipelines (cloud-native logging services, SIEM integration, log forwarding infrastructure) are provisioned by the platform-layer infrastructure team, not by the Golden Path infrastructure module. Golden Path authors must confirm the platform-level AU controls are active for the target environment but are not responsible for implementing them in the path module

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#pattern-description]

### Pattern Description

A conforming Golden Path infrastructure module is an IaC child module stored at `catalog/infrastructure/{path-id}/` that, when applied to a target environment, produces a fully specified workload isolation boundary, a per-path identity binding, and a compliance-traceable resource inventory. The module satisfies this pattern when it contains all three mandatory provision categories, exposes the four required outputs with correct sensitivity declarations, and passes TF-001 through TF-006 on every Terraform plan evaluation. An `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` at the module root declares the provision categories, required output names, and TF check IDs, giving ARB reviewers a machine-readable record of what the module claims to satisfy.

The three provision categories define the structural minimum that every conforming module must implement, regardless of technology profile:

- **Workload Isolation Boundary**: Provisions a dedicated runtime boundary for the workload with the enforcement baseline encoded as a path constant (not a consumer input). The enforcement baseline prevents unrestricted execution within the boundary (e.g., Kubernetes: namespace with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` label; ECS: task definition with security group isolation; Lambda: function resource policy scoping execution context). Compliance scope, path_id, and environment attribution are applied to the boundary resource at provisioning time.
- **Workload Identity**: Creates a dedicated cloud provider identity resource (e.g., AKS: managed identity + federated identity credential; EKS: IAM role with OIDC trust policy; Lambda: execution role with trust policy) with a least-privilege role assignment scoped to the specific secrets store resource. The identity binding is constrained to the exact workload execution context the security template will configure — no shared identities, no broad role assignments.
- **Resource Attribution**: Applies `compliance_scope`, `path_id`, `environment`, and `team` tags to every provisioned resource. Enables compliance dashboard queries, audit evidence tracing, and ZTA asset inventory requirements.

The four required outputs — `namespace_name`, `workload_identity_ref`, `secrets_store_uri`, `isolation_enforcement_level` — are the handoff payload from the infrastructure module author to the security template and scaffold authors. These are path constants: values encoded at the catalog level that the security template's workload identity artifact and the scaffold's secret management artifact consume without knowledge of the underlying resource names, subscription IDs, or account identifiers. ZTA compliance and NIST 800-53 r5 control coverage are outcomes of correctly implementing these provision categories, not structural drivers.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#architecture-diagram]

### Architecture Diagram

```
catalog/infrastructure/{path-id}/
├── infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml    ← Declares provision categories, required outputs, TF check IDs
├── main.tf                                ← Resource definitions for all three provision categories
├── variables.tf                           ← Consumer inputs (service_name, team, environment) + path constants
└── outputs.tf                             ← Four required outputs: namespace_name, workload_identity_ref,
                                             secrets_store_uri, isolation_enforcement_level

    Zero Trust Architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — infrastructure layer
    Secured by NIST SP 800-53 r5 | HIPAA • ARC-AMPE • FedRAMP Moderate overlays
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  1. Workload Isolation Boundary  NIST: AC-6, CM-6, CM-7          │
    │     ZTA: Assume breach — execution blast radius minimized       │
    │           at infrastructure layer, before any workload runs     │
    │     Dedicated runtime boundary with enforcement baseline        │
    │     encoded as a path constant (not consumer overridable).      │
    │     Compliance scope, path_id, environment labels applied.      │
    │     Examples by technology profile:                             │
    │       K8s: namespace + pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label  │
    │       ECS: task cluster + security group isolation config        │
    │       Lambda: function resource policy + execution scope const   │
    │       MFE: CDN origin + storage bucket policy                    │
    │     Policy checks: TF-001 (enforcement baseline), TF-005 (tags) │
    ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │  2. Workload Identity           NIST: IA-9, AC-6                │
    │     ZTA: Tenets 3, 6 — per-workload scoped, dynamically        │
    │           verified identity; no shared credentials             │
    │     Dedicated identity resource with least-privilege role       │
    │     scoped to the specific secrets store resource. Identity     │
    │     binding constrained to the workload execution context.     │
    │     Examples by technology profile:                             │
    │       K8s+Azure: managed identity + federated identity credential│
    │       K8s+AWS: IAM role + OIDC trust policy (IRSA)              │
    │       Lambda: execution role + trust policy (function ARN)      │
    │       ECS: task execution role + task IAM role                  │
    │     Policy checks: TF-002 (dedicated), TF-003 (binding scope),  │
    │                     TF-004 (role scope), TF-006 (sensitivity)   │
    ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │  3. Resource Attribution        NIST: CM-8                      │
    │     ZTA: Asset inventory — complete resource enumeration        │
    │           required for ZTA resource inventory and audit         │
    │     All resources tagged: compliance_scope, path_id,            │
    │     environment, team. Enables compliance dashboard queries.    │
    │     Policy check: TF-005 (all required tags present)           │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    Four required module outputs (path constants → security template and scaffold inputs)
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  namespace_name              → isolation boundary name consumed by identity and secret artifacts  │
    │  workload_identity_ref       → workload identity credential reference (sensitive)                 │
    │   Examples: K8s+Azure: client_id | K8s+AWS: role_arn | Lambda/ECS: role_arn    sensitive = true  │
    │  secrets_store_uri           → secrets store address consumed by secret management artifact       │
    │   Examples: Azure: key_vault_uri | AWS: secrets_manager_arn                    sensitive = true  │
    │  isolation_enforcement_level → compliance metadata and security template context                  │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#components]

### Components

| Component | Responsibility | Security Relevance | TF Check(s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` | Declares the module's provision categories, required outputs, and TF plan check IDs. Consumed by the ARB review process to verify completeness against this pattern. | Platform-agnostic YAML; confirms the module claims to satisfy all three provision categories | PTN-GOV-AI-003 |
| **Workload Isolation Boundary resource** | Provisions a dedicated runtime boundary with the enforcement baseline configuration encoded as a path constant — not a consumer input. Applies `path_id`, `compliance_scope`, and `environment` attribution. Technology-profile examples: Kubernetes namespace with PSA enforcement label; ECS task cluster with security group isolation; Lambda function resource policy. | Enforces ZTA Assume Breach tenet at infrastructure layer; prevents unrestricted execution before any workload is deployed | TF-001, TF-005 |
| **Cloud Provider Identity Resource** | Creates a dedicated, path-scoped identity for the workload. Not a shared platform identity. Name must be unique to the path and include `path_id` as a component. Technology-profile examples: Azure managed identity (AKS); IAM role with OIDC trust policy (EKS/Lambda); GCP service account (GKE). | Satisfies ZTA Tenet 6 (verify explicitly); uniquely identifies each workload at the identity layer | TF-002 |
| **Workload Identity Binding** | Constrains the cloud provider identity to the specific workload execution context. The binding scope must match the execution context the security template will configure. Technology-profile examples: Azure federated identity credential bound to K8s service account; IAM role OIDC trust condition scoped to function ARN; ECS task role trust policy. | Enforces ZTA per-session identity (Tenet 3); prevents identity token from being used by a different execution context | TF-003 |
| **Least-Privilege Role Assignment** | Grants the workload identity read access to the specific secrets store resource only — not the resource group, account root, or subscription. Technology-profile examples: Azure `Key Vault Secrets User` scoped to Key Vault resource ID; AWS IAM policy with `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on specific Secret ARN. | Satisfies ZTA Assume Breach (minimum blast radius at privilege scope); NIST AC-6 (Least Privilege) | TF-004 |
| **Resource Attribution Tags** | All IaC resources tagged with `compliance_scope`, `path_id`, `environment`, `team`. Required by TF-005 for all cloud provider resources in the module. | Satisfies NIST CM-8 (Information System Component Inventory); enables compliance dashboard queries and audit evidence tracing | TF-005 |
| **Module Outputs** | Four required outputs exposed with correct sensitivity declarations. `workload_identity_ref` and `secrets_store_uri` are `sensitive = true`. No output may use `sensitive = false` to override a sensitive source value. | Prevents accidental logging of identity credentials in CI/CD pipeline output; TF-006 asserts no sensitive override | TF-006 |

> **Note on the secrets management service**: The secrets management service (Azure: Key Vault; AWS: Secrets Manager; GCP: Secret Manager) is provisioned by the platform infrastructure team, not by the Golden Path infrastructure module. The module provisions least-privilege access to an existing secrets store and outputs its URI or ARN. Golden Path authors must confirm the secrets store address with the Platform Engineering team before encoding it as a path constant in `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` and `variables.tf`.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#interactions]

### Interactions

1. The Verification Contract author finalizes TF-001 through TF-006 check IDs before infrastructure module authoring begins (GUID-GOV-IMPL-001 Phase 4). Each TF check must be present in the contract before the module can be validated against it.
2. The infrastructure module author provisions a reference environment from the module and confirms all four required outputs are populated with non-placeholder values.
3. The Terraform plan JSON is generated with `terraform show -json` and evaluated against TF-001 through TF-006 using `opa eval`. All checks must pass.
4. The four required output values are delivered to the security template author (GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001 Phase 6 → GUID-SEC-IMPL-001 Phase 1): the workload identity credential reference (`workload_identity_ref`; e.g., managed identity client ID on AKS, IAM role ARN on EKS) is embedded as the path constant in the workload identity artifact; the secrets store address (`secrets_store_uri`; e.g., Key Vault URI on AKS, Secrets Manager ARN on EKS) is embedded in the secret management artifact.
5. At service instantiation, the CI/CD pipeline invokes the infrastructure module with `service_name` and `team` as consumer inputs. All security-bearing values are path constants in `variables.tf` — the consumer cannot override the isolation enforcement level, identity naming convention, or role assignment scope.
6. After `terraform apply`, the Verification Contract Layer 3 checks re-run against the live infrastructure state before the workload artifacts are applied.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#variations]

### Variations

**FedRAMP Moderate paths**: All three provision categories are required. Secrets store must have deletion protection enabled and a minimum soft-delete retention period. Role assignment scope must be at the specific secrets store resource level, not the resource group or account root. Add TF-007 (deletion protection) and TF-008 (retention policy) to the Verification Contract. Paths must declare `compliance_scope = "fedramp-moderate"` in `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml`.

**ARC-AMPE paths (CMS Medicaid / Medicare PHI environments)**: All three provision categories are required. ARC-AMPE is co-applicable with HIPAA for CMS-administered workloads — declare `compliance_scope = ["arc-ampe", "hipaa"]`. Resource attribution tags must include `arc_ampe_scope = "true"` as an additional required tag. The identity resource naming convention must include the ARC-AMPE program identifier. See ADR-SEC-001 for enterprise ZTA + ARC-AMPE enforcement context.

**Non-Kubernetes paths (ECS, Lambda, MFE/CDN, Batch)**: All three provision categories still apply. The Workload Isolation Boundary resource type and the Workload Identity binding mechanism differ by technology profile, but the obligations — enforcement baseline as a path constant, dedicated non-shared identity, identity binding scoped to the workload execution context — are identical. The four required output names and sensitivity declarations do not change. TF-001 through TF-006 check IDs apply to the equivalent resources for the technology profile. See GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001 for technology-profile-specific implementation guidance.

**Batch/worker paths (no HTTP ingress)**: All three provision categories still apply. The workload isolation boundary enforcement level remains at the path-constant baseline. The workload identity binding scope pattern is the same. Worker isolation boundaries may require additional egress attribution labels for job scheduling infrastructure. Document these as path constants in `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml`.

### Prerequisites

- Verification Contract TF check IDs (TF-001 through TF-006) are finalized before infrastructure module authoring begins — TF check IDs must be referenced in `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml`
- Target platform environment (e.g., Kubernetes cluster, ECS cluster, Lambda environment, CDN distribution) is provisioned by the platform infrastructure team; the module does not create the platform, only workload-level resources within it
- Secrets management service for the target environment is provisioned and its address confirmed with the Platform Engineering team before encoding as a path constant in `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` and `variables.tf`
- Platform-level workload identity federation is enabled on the target environment; the identity federation endpoint (e.g., cluster OIDC issuer URL for Kubernetes, trust anchor for Lambda) is available for workload identity binding configuration
- IaC module registry for the path's technology profile is accessible; provider version pinning confirmed with the Platform Infrastructure team
- The policy evaluation toolchain (`terraform`, `opa eval`) for the path's technology profile is available in the catalog CI/CD environment

#### Phase 1: Module Root and Manifest Declaration

1. Create `catalog/infrastructure/{path-id}/infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` declaring the provision categories, the four required outputs, and the TF plan check IDs from the Verification Contract. This is the ARB reviewer's checklist for the infrastructure module.
2. Create `variables.tf` with the three consumer inputs (`service_name`, `team`, `environment`) and all path constants (`compliance_scope`, `isolation_enforcement_level`, and any technology-profile-specific constants such as identity name prefix, secrets store address, or isolation boundary configuration value). Path constants use `default` values that are set to the approved organizational defaults and must not be consumer-overridable.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#phase-2-workload-isolation-boundary]

#### Phase 2: Workload Isolation Boundary

3. Author the isolation boundary resource in `main.tf` for the path's technology profile. The enforcement baseline configuration is a path constant — not derived from any consumer variable. Set the `path_id`, `compliance_scope`, and `environment` attribution on the boundary resource. Technology-profile examples: Kubernetes `kubernetes_namespace` with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` label; ECS task cluster with security group isolation configuration; Lambda function resource policy with execution scope constraints.
4. Validate against TF-001: run `terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan | opa eval --data policy-bundle/ --stdin-input 'data.{path_id}.tf001.allow'`. Must return `true` before proceeding.
page_texts.25:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#phase-3-workload-identity]

#### Phase 3: Workload Identity

5. Author the cloud provider identity resource for the path's technology profile. The identity name must include `var.path_id` and `var.service_name` as components — it must not be a generic shared name. Technology-profile examples: Azure managed identity (`azurerm_user_assigned_identity` for AKS); IAM role with OIDC trust policy (`aws_iam_role` for EKS or Lambda); GCP service account (`google_service_account` for GKE).
6. Author the workload identity binding that constrains the identity to the specific workload execution context. The binding scope must exactly match the execution context the security template will configure — if the execution context name is derived from a scaffold parameter (e.g., `${{ values.service_name }}`), the binding must use the same format. Technology-profile examples: Azure federated identity credential (`azurerm_federated_identity_credential`) bound to `system:serviceaccount:{namespace}:{service_name}`; IAM role OIDC trust condition scoped to the Kubernetes service account `sub` claim; Lambda execution role trust policy scoped to the function ARN.
7. Author the least-privilege role assignment scoped to the specific secrets store resource — not the resource group, account root, or subscription. Technology-profile examples: `azurerm_role_assignment` with `Key Vault Secrets User` scoped to the Key Vault resource ID; `aws_iam_policy` with `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on the specific Secret ARN.
8. Validate TF-002, TF-003, TF-004 in sequence using `opa eval`. All three must return `true`.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#example-1-module-root-structure]

#### Example 1: Module Root Structure

Every conforming Golden Path infrastructure module follows this directory structure regardless of technology profile:

```
catalog/infrastructure/{path-id}/
├── infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml   ← Provision categories, TF check IDs, required outputs
├── main.tf                               ← Three provision category resource blocks + locals
│     # ── Path constants (not consumer overridable) ──────────────────────
│     locals { isolation_enforcement_level, compliance_scope, identity_name_prefix, required_tags }
│
│     # ── 1. Workload Isolation Boundary (TF-001, TF-005) ─────────────────────
│     # Enforcement baseline as path constant — technology-profile-specific resource type
│     # K8s: kubernetes_namespace + pod-security label  |  ECS: cluster + SG config
│     # Lambda: function resource policy  |  MFE: storage policy + CDN OAI
│
│     # ── 2a. Cloud Provider Identity Resource (TF-002) ──────────────────────
│     # K8s+Azure: azurerm_user_assigned_identity
│     # K8s+AWS / Lambda / ECS: aws_iam_role (OIDC trust / function trust)
│     # GKE: google_service_account + Workload Identity binding
│
│     # ── 2b. Workload Identity Binding (TF-003) ──────────────────────
│     # Binding scope must match the workload execution context exactly
│     # K8s+Azure: azurerm_federated_identity_credential
│     # K8s+AWS: OIDC trust condition on aws_iam_role
│     # Lambda: function ARN trust condition in IAM role trust policy
│
│     # ── 2c. Least-Privilege Role Assignment (TF-004) ────────────────────
│     # Scope: specific secrets store resource only, not account/subscription root
│     # Azure: azurerm_role_assignment (Key Vault Secrets User, Key Vault resource ID)
│     # AWS: aws_iam_policy (secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, specific Secret ARN)
│
├── variables.tf                          ← Consumer inputs: service_name, team, environment
│                                           Path constants: compliance_scope, isolation_enforcement_level
└── outputs.tf                            ← Four required outputs (see below)
      namespace_name                (not sensitive)
      workload_identity_ref         (sensitive = true)  # K8s+Azure: client_id  |  AWS: role_arn
      secrets_store_uri             (sensitive = true)  # Azure: key_vault_uri  |  AWS: secret_arn
      isolation_enforcement_level   (not sensitive)
```

For platform-specific HCL implementation, see [GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001](../../../strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md).

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#best-practices]

### Best Practices

- **Provision the infrastructure module against a staging environment before authoring the security template.** The workload identity credential reference and `namespace_name` outputs are required inputs to the security template authoring phase. Authoring the security template with placeholder values and substituting them later introduces the most common failure mode: placeholder credential values in the workload identity artifact that produce silent authentication failures in the secrets operator at runtime.
- **Validate TF checks after each provision phase, not at the end.** `terraform plan | opa eval` per phase surfaces check failures while the relevant code is on screen. A batch validation at the end of a three-phase authoring session produces multiple concurrent failures across different resource types that are harder to diagnose in sequence.
- **Pin all provider versions explicitly.** Unversioned provider references in `required_providers` can silently break on the next `terraform init` following a provider release. Use `~>` version constraints pinned to the minor version (e.g., `~> 3.90`) and test provider upgrades explicitly before updating the catalog module.
- **Never add `sensitive = false` to override an output that references a workload identity credential or secrets store URI.** CI/CD pipeline logs are not encrypted at rest in all environments. A credential reference in plain text in a pipeline log is not a credential theft vector alone, but it is an enumeration aid. TF-006 asserts this is prohibited.
- **Document the engineering reasoning for the role choice in a code comment.** A future author who sees a least-privilege role (e.g., `Key Vault Secrets User` on Azure; a Secrets Manager read-only policy on AWS) without context may escalate it to a broader role for perceived reliability. A comment explaining that the read-only role satisfies the workload's only required access prevents this escalation pattern.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#common-pitfalls]

### Common Pitfalls

- **Workload identity binding scope does not match the workload execution context.** The identity binding must be scoped to the exact execution context the security template will configure. If the scaffold generates execution contexts named `{service_name}-sa` but the binding references just `{service_name}`, the identity token exchange is rejected silently — the workload starts, secrets reconciliation fails, and secrets are never synced. Confirm the exact execution context identifier format with the scaffold author before authoring the identity binding. Technology-profile examples: Kubernetes FIC subject must match `system:serviceaccount:{namespace}:{service_account_name}`; Lambda trust policy condition must match the function ARN.
- **Enforcement baseline configuration applied to the wrong resource type.** The enforcement baseline must be applied to the isolation boundary resource, not to an individual workload artifact or child resource. Applied to the wrong resource type, the configuration has no enforcement effect. After `terraform apply`, verify the enforcement baseline is active on the isolation boundary resource using the platform-appropriate inspection command (e.g., Kubernetes: `kubectl get ns {namespace} --show-labels`). The Layer 2a fitness function catches this failure at staging apply time.
- **Scoping the role assignment too broadly.** Assigning least-privilege secrets access at the subscription, account, or resource group scope (rather than the specific secrets store resource) grants the workload identity access to every secrets store in that scope. This violates ZTA Assume Breach (minimize blast radius) and NIST AC-6. Scope must be the specific secrets store resource ID or ARN (Azure: Key Vault resource ID; AWS: specific Secret ARN).
- **Using an empty string default for the workload identity credential output.** An empty string default in `outputs.tf` means a module that failed to create the identity resource still produces output — just an empty string. The security template author then uses an empty string as the annotation value, which produces a pod that starts but has no workload identity. Required outputs must have no default value; a missing resource should produce a Terraform error, not a silent empty output.
- **Omitting the `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml`.** Without this file, the ARB has no machine-readable record of which provision categories the module claims to satisfy or which TF check IDs validate them. PTN-GOV-AI-001 ARB checklist requires all template components to be present — a module without its manifest is treated as incomplete.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#standards-alignment]

### Standards Alignment

Zero Trust Architecture (NIST SP 800-207) is the governing security design principle for this pattern. NIST SP 800-53 r5 is the normative control framework that operationalizes ZTA tenets at the infrastructure resource level. The six Terraform plan OPA checks assert compliance with these controls on every Terraform plan evaluation.

| NIST 800-53 r5 Control | Control Name | Infrastructure Provision Category | ZTA Tenet (NIST SP 800-207) | TF Check(s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AC-6 | Least Privilege | **Workload Identity** — role assignment scoped to secrets read access on the specific secrets store resource only, not a broad account or subscription role | Assume Breach: Minimum blast radius at privilege scope | TF-004 |
| IA-9 | Service Identification and Authentication | **Workload Identity** — dedicated identity per workload; identity binding scoped to specific workload execution context | Tenets 3, 6: Per-session access; dynamically enforced per-workload identity | TF-002, TF-003 |
| CM-6 | Configuration Settings | **Workload Isolation Boundary** — enforcement baseline configuration is a path constant; cannot be weakened without a Terraform plan change | Assume Breach: Immutable baseline prevents configuration drift | TF-001 |
| CM-7 | Least Functionality | **Workload Isolation Boundary** — enforcement baseline eliminates unrestricted execution within the boundary (e.g., K8s: blocks root execution, privilege escalation, and host path access at namespace level) | Assume Breach: Minimize blast radius through boundary-level execution control | TF-001 |
| CM-8 | Information System Component Inventory | **Resource Attribution** — all resources carry compliance_scope, path_id, environment, team tags for inventory and audit evidence queries | ZTA Asset Inventory: Complete resource enumeration required for ZTA resource inventory | TF-005 |
| SC-28 | Protection of Information at Rest | Least-privilege role assignment grants read-only access to an already-encrypted secrets store; secrets store encryption is a platform prerequisite | Assume Breach: Data at rest encrypted; breach does not expose plaintext secrets | — (platform prerequisite) |

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#compliance-requirements]

### Compliance Requirements

Zero Trust Architecture (NIST SP 800-207) is the governing design principle at the infrastructure layer. The three mandatory provision categories implement ZTA tenets before any workload is deployed — trust is established at provisioning time, not at runtime. NIST SP 800-53 r5 is the normative control framework that operationalizes ZTA at the Terraform resource level. HIPAA, ARC-AMPE, and FedRAMP Moderate are regulatory overlays that satisfy their requirements by mapping to the NIST controls above.

The ARB review must include explicit sign-off from the Infrastructure Architecture representative confirming that the isolation boundary enforcement baseline configuration, identity resource naming convention, role assignment scope, and required tag set are correctly configured for the path's compliance scope and technology profile.

All infrastructure module configurations are path-level constants — they apply to every service instantiated from the path. Any team that needs to deviate (e.g., additional IAM permissions, alternative Key Vault scope) must submit a formal exception request (GUID-GOV-PROC-002) reviewed by Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture jointly.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#approval-process]

### Approval Process

- **New infrastructure module (first publication)**: Platform Engineering review → Infrastructure Architecture review → Security Architecture sign-off → ARB approval as part of complete Golden Path bundle
- **Workload identity change (any version)**: Security Architecture review required regardless of whether the change is breaking — identity resource naming, binding scope, or role assignment changes are never processed under lightweight minor-version review
- **Isolation enforcement level change**: Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture joint review required. Enforcement level changes affect the workload security posture of every service on the path
- **Emergency security patch (CVE affecting Terraform provider affecting managed identity behavior)**: Express review; Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture sign-off in lieu of full ARB; 48-hour SLA

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#monitoring-and-metrics]

### Monitoring and Metrics

The metrics below span all four verification layers. Layer 3 metrics are generated continuously by CI/CD pipeline execution. Layer 4 metrics are generated continuously by the runtime monitoring infrastructure — they are only possible because conforming modules apply the required tags and naming conventions that allow the monitoring layer to attribute resources to a specific path.

| Metric | Verification Layer | Target | Measurement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Required module files present at `catalog/infrastructure/{path-id}/` | Layer 1 | 100% | Conformance gate result in CI/CD pipeline |
| Layer 2a: Isolation enforcement baseline active on isolation boundary post-apply | Layer 2 | 100% | `isolation-baseline-{path-id}-{version}.txt` in compliance evidence store |
| Layer 2b: Workload identity chain test passes (ESO secret sync) | Layer 2 | 100% | `identity-chain-{path-id}-{version}.txt` in compliance evidence store |
| Verification Contract TF check pass rate on Terraform plan evaluations | Layer 3 | 100% | `opa-evidence-{path-id}-{version}.json` in compliance evidence store |
| Isolation enforcement violations detected post-deploy | Layer 4 | 0 | Platform-appropriate drift detection rule on isolation boundary resource (e.g., `kubectl get events --field-selector=reason=FailedCreate` for K8s admission rejections; AWS Config rule on ECS task security groups) |
| Workload identity authentication failures (secrets reconciliation failures) | Layer 4 | 0 | Secrets reconciliation operator `SecretSyncError` alert or equivalent in platform monitoring; `path_id` label required for attribution |
| Role assignments outside approved role list | Layer 4 | 0 | Azure Policy / AWS Config rule on role assignment role definition; requires `path_id` tag on role assignment resource |
| Infrastructure resource drift from declared Terraform state | Layer 4 | 0 | AWS Config / Azure Policy drift detection rules on path-tagged resources |

---

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#real-world-example-1-first-arb-submission--gp-001-infrastructure-module]

### Real-World Example 1: First ARB Submission — GP-001 Infrastructure Module

**Context:** Platform Engineering is authoring the complete GP-001 bundle. The infrastructure module is authored before the security template because its outputs are required inputs to the security template authoring phase.

**Implementation:** The infrastructure module author co-defines TF-001 through TF-006 check assertions with the Verification Contract author (GUID-GOV-IMPL-001 Phase 4), confirming Rego JSON path expressions against the technology-profile-specific resource plan shapes. They author the isolation boundary resource (enforcement baseline as path constant, `HIPAA` compliance scope label), the dedicated identity resource for GP-001, the identity binding constrained to the workload execution context (`{service_name}@{namespace}` or equivalent for the technology profile), and the least-privilege secrets store role assignment. All four required outputs are populated. The Terraform plan JSON is evaluated against TF-001 through TF-006 — all pass. After `terraform apply` to staging, both Layer 2 fitness functions pass: isolation enforcement baseline confirmed active on the boundary resource; identity chain test confirms secrets reconciliation succeeds. `workload_identity_ref` output value is delivered to the security template author as the workload identity path constant. All Phase 6 evidence submitted to the compliance evidence store.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#real-world-example-2-promoting-a-path-from-hipaa-to-arc-ampe-co-scope]

### Real-World Example 2: Promoting a Path from HIPAA to ARC-AMPE Co-Scope

**Context:** An existing GP-001 HIPAA path must be extended for a CMS Medicaid workload requiring ARC-AMPE compliance. The infrastructure module must be updated to satisfy ARC-AMPE requirements.

**Implementation:** The `compliance_scope` local is updated from `"HIPAA"` to `["HIPAA", "ARC-AMPE"]`. Resource attribution tags are updated to include `arc_ampe_scope = "true"`. The identity resource naming convention is updated to include the ARC-AMPE program identifier. Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture jointly review the changes. A new TF-007 check is added to the Verification Contract: `arc_ampe_scope` tag must equal `"true"` on all resources. ARB approves the updated bundle as GP-001 v2.0.0 (minor version — no breaking output changes).

**Outcome:** Services on GP-001 v2.0.0 enter production with ARC-AMPE resource tagging and compliance scope active from the first Terraform apply. The compliance metadata file is updated to record the ARC-AMPE → NIST crosswalk per GUID-GOV-IMPL-002.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#scenario-1-new-language-variant--same-infrastructure-new-scaffold]

#### Scenario 1: New Language Variant — Same Infrastructure, New Scaffold

A new path GP-010 needs an infrastructure module. The Platform Engineering team identifies that GP-010's infrastructure requirements are identical to GP-001 for the same technology profile — same isolation enforcement baseline, same identity pattern, same secrets store scope. They author GP-010's infrastructure module by adapting GP-001's `main.tf` and `variables.tf` (Approach 2 in GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001): update `path_id` throughout, update the identity name prefix, confirm the Verification Contract TF check Rego path expressions still resolve against the GP-010 plan JSON, re-run all TF checks against the GP-010 staging Terraform plan. All checks pass. Both Layer 2 fitness functions pass. The `workload_identity_ref` output value differs from GP-001 because the identity resource is a different cloud resource, but the output name and semantics are identical. The security template author for GP-010 uses the same workload identity artifact structure with the new credential reference value.
page_texts.46:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#scenario-2-infrastructure-module-output-missing-from-security-template]

#### Scenario 2: Infrastructure Module Output Missing from Security Template

During security template authoring for GP-002, the security template author discovers that the `workload_identity_ref` output from the infrastructure module is an empty string in the staging environment. Investigation reveals the infrastructure module's identity resource was created but `outputs.tf` references a non-existent local variable. The module was applied but the output was never populated. TF-006 is designed to catch this: an output with no real source value should fail the Terraform plan check, not silently produce an empty string. Additionally, the Layer 2b fitness function (identity chain test) would also have caught this — the secrets reconciliation attempt would have failed with a credential error. The infrastructure module is corrected; TF-006 now passes; the Layer 2b fitness function passes; the security template author receives the correct `workload_identity_ref` value.
page_texts.48:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#before-problem-state]

#### Before (Problem State)

Without an infrastructure module specification, Platform Engineering authors each path's IaC module against memory and convention. Some paths receive a correctly configured isolation boundary; others miss the enforcement baseline configuration because it is not salient in the resource definition and is not included in any checklist. Some paths receive a dedicated identity with a correctly scoped binding; others reference a shared platform identity or produce a binding with an overly broad execution context scope. When the infrastructure module author delivers the module to staging without an output contract, the security template author and scaffold author have no `workload_identity_ref` or `secrets_store_uri` to reference — they either embed placeholder values and proceed, or stop work and wait for the infrastructure author to re-deliver.

A bundle assembled from placeholder values cannot be instantiated correctly. A placeholder credential reference in the workload identity artifact passes syntactic validation but produces a workload that starts and then fails silently: the secrets reconciliation operator cannot authenticate to the secrets store because the identity binding value is empty, and secrets are never synced. The failure is not a crash; it is a misconfigured workload in production with no error surface. An autonomous AI agent instantiating a service from an incompletely specified path produces the same outcome — a workload that starts but cannot function, with no mechanism to detect the gap from the service repository.

Paths accumulate these inconsistencies across the catalog. Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture review each module individually before ARB, finding the same gaps per path rather than reviewing a specification once. ARB reviews for complete bundles are delayed until the infrastructure module is corrected and the security template and scaffold authors update their artifacts with the corrected values.
page_texts.49:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#after-solution-state]

#### After (Solution State)

With a conforming infrastructure module, every path enters ARB with evidence across all four verification layers: Layer 1 gate passed (required files present); Layer 2 fitness functions passed (isolation enforcement baseline confirmed active on the boundary resource, identity chain test confirmed secrets reconciliation functional); Layer 3 TF checks all passed (isolation boundary enforcement baseline, dedicated identity resource, scoped identity binding, least-privilege secrets access, required attribution tags, output sensitivity); Layer 4 design obligations met (all resources carry required tags and identity resource name includes `path_id` for runtime drift attribution). Security Architecture reviews the module once at the catalog level. The security template author receives the correct `workload_identity_ref` value and authors the workload identity artifact with the correct credential reference. The first service instantiated from the path enters production with workload identity active and runtime drift monitoring enabled.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md#tldr]

## TL;DR

**Problem:** The infrastructure module is one of five mandatory Golden Path bundle components, but no specification defines what it must provision or what outputs it must expose. Platform Engineering authors modules ad hoc — provision content varies between paths, security-bearing configurations are left as consumer-supplied inputs rather than path constants, outputs are missing or inconsistently named. Security template and scaffold authors are blocked waiting for module output values that may never be delivered correctly until the infrastructure module is remediated and re-applied. Paths with incomplete infrastructure modules cannot be submitted to the ARB, and autonomous AI agents consuming those paths produce workloads that start but fail silently.

**Solution:** This pattern defines the mandatory provision categories (Workload Isolation Boundary, Workload Identity, Resource Attribution), required output contract (four outputs with correct sensitivity declarations), and six IaC plan OPA checks (TF-001 through TF-006) that every Golden Path infrastructure module must satisfy before ARB submission. A conforming module stores an `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` at the module root declaring its provision categories and TF check IDs, giving ARB reviewers a machine-readable conformance record. Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture review the specification once at the catalog level; every path whose module conforms inherits that review.

**When to Use:**
- Authoring the infrastructure module component for a new Golden Path bundle before ARB submission
- Auditing an existing path's infrastructure module for conformance with this specification prior to re-submission or compliance review
- Remediating an ad hoc catalog module whose missing outputs are blocking security template or scaffold authoring
- Extending a path's infrastructure module for a new compliance scope (ARC-AMPE, FedRAMP Moderate)

**Key Benefits:**
- Security template and scaffold authors receive the four required output values — workload identity credential reference, secrets store address, isolation boundary name, isolation enforcement level — as path constants with no placeholder values, because the module must pass TF-001 through TF-006 before any author dependency can be declared satisfied
- The isolation enforcement baseline is declared at the infrastructure layer — it cannot be absent from the boundary resource without a Terraform plan check failure (TF-001), regardless of technology profile
- Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture review the specification once; every conforming path inherits NIST 800-53 r5 control evidence and — by overlay — HIPAA, ARC-AMPE, and FedRAMP Moderate compliance evidence automatically

**Implementation Complexity:** Medium

**Prerequisites:** Verification Contract TF check IDs finalized (GUID-GOV-IMPL-001 Phase 4); target platform environment provisioned with workload identity federation enabled; secrets store address confirmed with Platform Engineering before authoring begins

**Related Patterns:** PTN-INFRA-API-006, PTN-SEC-GOV-001, PTN-APP-GOV-004, PTN-GOV-AI-003, PTN-INFRA-GOV-002, PTN-SEC-K8S-004
